questions.title: Spring Data Specifications for Dynamic Queries
questions.question: How do you build dynamic, type-safe queries in Spring Data JPA using Specifications?
questions.direct_answer: **`Specification<T>`** is a functional interface returning a JPA `Predicate` — one filter per Specification, **composed at runtime** with `.and()`, `.or()`, `.not()`. Repositories that extend **`JpaSpecificationExecutor<T>`** gain `findAll(Specification, Pageable)`, `count`, and `findOne` methods. The win is killing the **combinatorial explosion** of derived methods for search forms — instead of `findByStatus`, `findByStatusAndCity`, `findByStatusAndDate`, … you have one `findAll(spec)` built from only the filters provided. Returning `null` is idiomatic for an empty filter. Generated SQL is **always parameterized** — safe from injection by construction. Trade-offs vs **QueryDSL**: Specifications are terser than raw Criteria but more verbose than QueryDSL's Q-classes; QueryDSL has superior compile-time type safety; Specifications win on zero extra build setup.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows alternatives to writing dozens of `findBy*And*Or*` methods for complex filter UIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing separate `findByStatusAndDateAndCity()`, `findByStatusAndDate()`, `findByDate()` methods for every combination — unmaintainable past three filters
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare Specifications against QueryDSL, mention the JPA metamodel for type-safe field references, and note that the generated SQL is always parameterized

sections.title: One `findBy` per Combination Doesn't Scale — Specifications Compose Instead
sections.content:
The moment a search form has **three optional filters** — status, date range, city — the derived-query approach breaks. You need `findByStatus`, `findByStatusAndDate`, `findByStatusAndCity`, `findByStatusAndDateAndCity`, and so on. **Seven methods for three filters.** Add a fourth and you need 15. Adding validation or logging multiplies the burden.

The **Specification** pattern composes individual predicates at runtime. Each filter is a reusable `Specification<T>` — a lambda producing a JPA Criteria predicate. Combine with `.and()`, `.or()`, `.not()` to build the final query dynamically.

Under the hood, Specifications wrap the **JPA Criteria API**.
- Generated SQL is always parameterized — **safe from SQL injection by construction**, unlike string-concatenated JPQL.
- The trade-off is verbosity — the Criteria API requires more code than a JPQL string for the same query — but the composability and runtime safety make it worth it for any non-trivial dynamic search.

sections.title: Building Composable Specifications — Repository, Predicates, Composition
Specifications vs QueryDSL vs Raw Criteria vs `@Query` Conditionals
sections.content:
Four common approaches to dynamic JPA queries. Each has a sweet spot.

| Approach | Setup cost | Type safety | Verbosity | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Specifications | Zero (built into Spring Data) | Partial (string field names) | Medium | Small-medium dynamic search; most apps |
| QueryDSL | Annotation processor + Q-classes | Full (Q-classes enforce names) | Low (fluent) | Complex search; teams accepting build step |
| Raw Criteria API | Zero | Partial | High | One-off advanced queries; metamodel use |
| `@Query` + `:p IS NULL OR ...` | Zero | None (string) | Low | Fixed queries with 2-3 optional filters |

sections.title: Production Pattern — Pagination, Joins, Fetch, and the Count-Query Guard
Pitfalls, Anti-Patterns, and the QueryDSL Migration Trigger
sections.content:
**When Specifications help:**
- **Dynamic search forms with 3+ optional filters** — one `findAll(spec, page)` replaces a dozen derived methods.
- **Reusable predicates** — same `hasStatus` powers `findAll`, `count`, `findOne`.
- **Always parameterized SQL** — no injection risk by construction.

**When Specifications hurt:**
- **String field names are fragile** — `root.get("stauts")` compiles, fails at runtime.
- **Verbose for simple cases** — for a single fixed filter, `findByStatus` is shorter and clearer.
- **Join duplication trap** — `root.join("customer")` from multiple Specifications produces multiple JOINs to the same table.

**Watch for:**
- **`fetch()` on collections breaks count queries** — guard with `if (q.getResultType() != Long.class)`.
- **`Specification.where(null).and(null)`** is idiomatic but easy to misread; helper methods make intent clearer.
- **Sort inside the data query, not the count query** — Spring Data handles this correctly only when the Specification doesn't try to manipulate `q.orderBy` on count queries.
- **JPA metamodel** (`Order_.status`) gives compile-time field names but adds a build step; at that cost you might as well adopt QueryDSL.

**When to migrate to QueryDSL:**
- More than ~10 filter methods with string field names.
- Recurring join-reuse bugs.
- Production typos in field names.
- Need compile-time validation of every query path.

sections.title: Decision Heuristic — Specifications, QueryDSL, or Something Else
sections.content:
**Use Specifications when:**
- Search UI has 3+ optional filters that combine independently.
- Filters span joins (customer name, product category).
- Team won't add a QueryDSL annotation processor.
- Predicates need to be composed and reused across `findAll`, `count`, `findOne`.

**Don't use Specifications when:**
- Only 1-2 fixed filters — derived query method is simpler.
- Recursive or CTE queries — native SQL via `@Query(nativeQuery=true)`.
- Reporting/analytics — raw JDBC or jOOQ for fine-grained SQL control.
- Building GraphQL resolvers — evaluate `graphql-jpa-query` or similar.

**Performance note:** Specifications compile to the same SQL as equivalent JPQL — no runtime overhead. The cost is at build time (slightly slower compilation due to Criteria type inference). Choose on **readability and composability**, never performance.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Specification<T>`** wraps a single `Predicate`; `.where().and().or()` composes them dynamically.
- **`null` is idiomatic** for an absent filter — `Specification.where(null)` is a no-op chain start.
- **`JpaSpecificationExecutor<T>`** must be added to the repository to enable `findAll(spec, page)`.
- **Always parameterized** — Criteria values become bind parameters; safe from injection.
- **Guard fetches on count queries** — `if (q.getResultType() != Long.class)` prevents the forbidden fetch-on-count error.
- **Use the JPA metamodel** (`Order_.status`) for compile-time field names; or graduate to QueryDSL.
- **QueryDSL wins past 10 filters** — Q-classes give compile-time validation and IDE autocomplete.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Specifications solve the dynamic query problem — building a WHERE clause where filters are optional and combinations depend on runtime input.

**The pattern:**
- Each filter is a `Specification<Order>` — a lambda returning a `Predicate`
- Compose with `Specification.where(hasStatus(status)).and(inCity(city)).and(after(date))`
- `null` predicates are ignored — if `status` is null, `hasStatus(null)` returns `null` and the chain skips it

**Implementation:**
- Add `JpaSpecificationExecutor<Order>` to the repository
- Define static factories returning `Specification<Order>`
- Call `orderRepo.findAll(spec, pageable)` — pagination and sorting work transparently

**vs QueryDSL:**
- QueryDSL generates a `QOrder` class from the entity at compile time
- `QOrder.order.status.eq(status).and(QOrder.order.city.eq(city))` — fluent and type-safe
- More powerful for path traversal; needs an annotation processor and Q-class generation step

**When to switch:**
- Past ~10 filter methods, string field names cause production typos
- Need compile-time validation — adopt QueryDSL or the JPA metamodel

questions.question: How do Spring Data JPA repository methods work — `findBy`, `@Query`, native queries, and derived methods?
questions.title: Spring Data JPA Repository Methods — Derived, JPQL, Native
questions.direct_answer: Spring Data JPA offers **three ways** to define query methods. **Derived queries** — names like `findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter` parsed into JPQL at startup — are validated early and need zero code, but become unreadable past ~3 parameters. **`@Query(JPQL)`** is explicit JPQL with **`@Param`**, validated at startup, supports joins/aggregations/projections, and keeps method names clean. **`@Query(value=..., nativeQuery=true)`** drops to database-specific SQL for window functions, CTEs, full-text, JSON operators — at the cost of runtime-only validation, no portability, and no L2 cache. **`@Modifying`** is required for UPDATE/DELETE (`clearAutomatically=true` flushes the persistence context after, `flushAutomatically=true` flushes before). Pagination works everywhere via a trailing `Pageable`; native queries additionally need `countQuery="..."`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the three query definition approaches and their trade-offs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating long derived method names like `findByStatusAndCityAndCreatedAtAfterAndPriceLessThan` instead of using `@Query` for complex queries
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the query derivation mechanism, mention `@Param` for named parameters, projections for list views, and when derived queries become unmaintainable

sections.title: Spring Data Writes Your SQL — Until the Method Name Becomes a Sentence
sections.content:
Spring Data's killer feature is **derived query methods** — declare `findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter(String status, LocalDate date)` and Spring generates the JPQL at startup from a well-defined naming convention. No implementation class, no SQL, no boilerplate.

This works beautifully for simple lookups. It breaks down when names become sentences: `findByStatusAndCityAndCreatedAtAfterAndPriceLessThanOrderByCreatedAtDesc`. The method name is now longer than the JPQL it would replace and harder to refactor.

**`@Query` is the escape hatch** — write the JPQL explicitly and name the method anything.
- For database-specific features (window functions, CTEs, full-text search, JSON operators), `@Query(nativeQuery=true)` drops to raw SQL.
- The trade-off: native queries bypass entity management and L2 cache, and they fail only at runtime.

sections.title: Derived vs `@Query` vs Native — Pick by Complexity
sections.content:
Match the query complexity to the definition approach.

| Aspect | Derived Method | `@Query` (JPQL) | `@Query` (Native) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Definition | Method name convention | Explicit JPQL | Raw SQL |
| Readability | Good for 1-2 conditions | Always clear | SQL-familiar |
| Validation | At startup (parse) | At startup (JPQL parse) | Runtime only |
| Portability | DB-agnostic | DB-agnostic | DB-specific |
| Joins / aggregations | Limited | Full JPQL | Full SQL |
| L2 cache integration | Full | Full | Bypasses |
| Best for | Simple `findBy` 1-2 fields | Joins, aggregations | Window fn, CTE, JSON |

sections.title: All Three Approaches — Same Use Case
sections.content:
'Active orders for a customer placed after a date, newest first' — three implementations.

**Derived (simplest, breaks past ~3 parameters):**

```java
List<Order> findByCustomerIdAndStatusAndCreatedAtAfterOrderByCreatedAtDesc(
    Long customerId, OrderStatus status, Instant after);
```

**`@Query` JPQL (readable, portable):**

```java
@Query("""
    SELECT o FROM Order o
    WHERE o.customer.id = :customerId
      AND o.status = :status
      AND o.createdAt > :after
    ORDER BY o.createdAt DESC
""")
List<Order> findRecentActive(@Param("customerId") Long customerId,
                             @Param("status") OrderStatus status,
                             @Param("after") Instant after);
```

**`@Query` native (database-specific):**

```java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT o.* FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = :cid AND o.status = :status AND o.created_at > :after
      AND o.metadata @> '{"priority":"HIGH"}'::jsonb
    ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
""",
    countQuery = """
    SELECT count(*) FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = :cid AND o.status = :status AND o.created_at > :after
      AND o.metadata @> '{"priority":"HIGH"}'::jsonb
""",
    nativeQuery = true)
Page<Order> findRecentHighPriority(@Param("cid") Long cid,
                                   @Param("status") String status,
                                   @Param("after") Instant after,
                                   Pageable page);
```

The Postgres JSONB `@>` operator can't be expressed in JPQL — native required. Note `countQuery` is mandatory for native `Page<T>`.

**`@Modifying` UPDATE/DELETE:**

```java
@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true, flushAutomatically = true)
@Query("UPDATE Order o SET o.status = :newStatus WHERE o.createdAt < :cutoff")
int archiveOlderThan(@Param("newStatus") OrderStatus newStatus,
                     @Param("cutoff") Instant cutoff);
```

- **`flushAutomatically=true`** — flushes pending writes before the UPDATE so in-flight changes apply.
- **`clearAutomatically=true`** — clears the persistence context after so the next `findById` doesn't return a stale cached entity.

sections.title: Projections, Pagination Safety, and Native-Query Discipline
sections.content:
**Interface projections for list views:**

```java
public interface OrderSummary {
    Long getId();
    String getStatus();
    BigDecimal getTotal();
}
List<OrderSummary> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);
```

- **Projects only the requested fields** — Spring generates a SELECT with just those columns.
- **No entity construction, no lazy proxies, no N+1** on lazy access.
- **Dynamic projection:** `<T> List<T> findByStatus(OrderStatus status, Class<T> type)` lets the caller pick `OrderSummary.class` or `Order.class` at runtime.

**`Page<T>` vs `Slice<T>`:**
- **`Page<T>`** runs two queries — data + COUNT. The COUNT can dominate latency on huge tables.
- **`Slice<T>`** fetches `pageSize+1` rows to infer `hasNext()` — no COUNT.
- Use `Slice<T>` for 'Load More' UIs that don't show 'Page 3 of 47'.

**Native query discipline:**
- **Each native query couples you to one database** — JSONB operators in Postgres are not portable.
- **Validation only at runtime** — typos slip into production until the code path runs.
- **Bypasses L2 cache** — frequent native reads can wipe out cache savings.
- **Guardrail:** require a code-review comment explaining why JPQL can't express it.

**Production checklist:**
- Derived queries only when method name fits ≤ 3 clauses.
- `@Param` always; never positional `?1`.
- `countQuery="..."` for every native `Page<T>`.
- Projection interfaces for every list view.
- `@Modifying(clearAutomatically=true, flushAutomatically=true)` for UPDATE/DELETE.
- `@Transactional` on the service method wrapping `@Modifying` calls.

sections.title: Decision Flow in Three Questions
sections.content:
**Q1 — How many filter conditions?**
- 1-2 required → **derived method** (`findByStatusAndCity`).
- 3+ required → **`@Query` JPQL**.
- Optional conditions → **Specifications** or **`@Query` with `:p IS NULL OR field = :p`**.

**Q2 — Database-specific features needed?**
- JPQL can express it → **`@Query` JPQL**.
- JSONB, window fn, full-text → **`@Query(nativeQuery=true)`**.
- DDL or `EXPLAIN` → **`JdbcClient`**, not a JPA repository.

**Q3 — Read or write?**
- Standard CRUD → inherited from `JpaRepository`.
- Bulk UPDATE/DELETE → `@Modifying @Query` with `clearAutomatically=true`.
- Batch inserts → `saveAll(...)` with `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size` configured.

**Common mistakes:**
- `@Modifying` without `@Transactional` — fails at runtime.
- Forgotten `countQuery` on native `Page<T>` — wrong totals.
- Returning full entities to API layer — leaks schema, triggers lazy loads.

sections.title: Trade-offs Across the Three Styles
sections.content:
**When derived methods help:**
- Self-documenting for simple lookups.
- Validated at startup — typos fail context load.
- Zero boilerplate.

**When derived methods hurt:**
- Past 3-4 conditions, the name is unreadable and unrefactorable.
- No support for aggregations, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions.
- Limited control over fetch joins.

**When `@Query` JPQL helps:**
- Explicit, readable, version-controlled SQL.
- Validated at startup against entity metadata.
- Full JPQL features — joins, projections, subqueries.

**When native SQL helps and hurts:**
- Helps: JSONB, window functions, CTEs, vendor extensions.
- Hurts: locks you to one database, fails only at runtime, bypasses L2 cache.

**Watch for:**
- **Positional parameters (`?1`)** — break silently when arguments are reordered.
- **`countQuery` missing** on native `Page<T>` — pagination math breaks.
- **JSONB and `LIMIT 1`** — native queries returning single rows still need explicit pagination or limit.
- **`@Modifying` without `clearAutomatically`** — stale cached entity served on next read.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Derived methods** validate at startup; **native queries** validate only at runtime.
- **`@Query` JPQL** validates against entity metadata at startup — typos fail context load.
- **`@Param("name")`** required for named parameters; prefer over positional `?1`.
- **`@Modifying`** is mandatory for UPDATE/DELETE; `clearAutomatically=true` prevents stale entity reads.
- **Interface projections** avoid loading full entities — Spring SELECTs only the requested fields.
- **`Page<T>` runs a COUNT; `Slice<T>` does not** — pick by whether the UI needs the total.
- **Native queries are technical debt** — couple you to one database; require runtime tests.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Data JPA offers three ways to define query methods, and the right choice depends on complexity.

**Derived method names:**
- Spring parses the name at startup and generates JPQL
- `findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter(String, Instant)` -> `WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ?`
- Validated at startup — non-existent fields fail context load
- Stop when names exceed 3-4 parts

**`@Query` JPQL:**
- Explicit, readable, supports aggregations, joins, projections
- Use `@Param` for named parameters; avoid positional
- Validated against entity metadata at startup

**`@Query(nativeQuery=true)`:**
- For database-specific features — JSONB, window functions, CTEs, full-text
- Fails only at runtime; bypasses L2 cache; locks you to one database
- Always provide `countQuery` for `Page<T>`

**Modifying queries:**
- `@Modifying` required for UPDATE/DELETE
- `clearAutomatically=true` prevents stale entity reads after the bulk update
- Always run inside a `@Transactional` boundary

**Production tips:**
- Use interface projections for list views — no entity construction, no lazy proxies
- `Slice<T>` instead of `Page<T>` for infinite scroll — skips the COUNT query
- Native queries need an integration test per query — runtime validation only

questions.question: How do you implement pagination and sorting with Spring Data JPA using `Pageable`, `Page`, and `Slice`?
questions.title: Pagination — Pageable, Page, Slice, and Keyset
questions.direct_answer: Spring Data accepts **`Pageable`** as the last argument; the return type decides whether COUNT runs. **`Page<T>`** runs **two queries** — data with `LIMIT/OFFSET` and `SELECT COUNT(*)`; the count is often as expensive as the data on large tables. **`Slice<T>`** runs **one query** for `pageSize+1` rows — `hasNext()` is true if the extra row exists; ideal for 'Load More' / infinite scroll. **`List<T>`** with `Pageable` works but loses metadata. For huge tables, **`OFFSET n` itself is O(n)** because the database scans and discards `n` rows; **keyset (cursor) pagination** stays constant-time. **`@Query(countQuery="...")`** lets you optimize the count separately. The **`JOIN FETCH` + `Pageable` trap (HHH90003004)** is the most common pagination bug — Hibernate paginates in memory.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the difference between Page and Slice, the COUNT cost, and keyset pagination
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using `Page` when `Slice` would suffice — COUNT on a million-row table can dwarf the data query
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain keyset pagination as an alternative to OFFSET for deep pagination, mention `countQuery` optimization, and the JOIN FETCH + Pageable trap

sections.title: The COUNT Query Is Often Slower Than the Data Query
sections.content:
Every `Page<T>` triggers **two SQL queries** — one for the data, one for `COUNT(*)`. On a multi-million-row table, the COUNT can take **longer than the data query** because the database scans the entire matching set; the data query stops at the LIMIT.

**`Slice<T>`** skips COUNT entirely. It fetches `size + 1` rows — if it gets more than `size`, there's a next page. Ideal for **infinite scroll** where 'page 3 of 47' isn't displayed.

Both `Page` and `Slice` accept a `Pageable` combining page number, page size, and sort. Spring Data translates this to `OFFSET` + `LIMIT`. APIs typically expose `?page=0&size=20&sort=createdAt,desc` — Spring resolves it to a `Pageable` automatically.

sections.title: Page vs Slice vs List vs Keyset
sections.content:
Four pagination strategies, four very different latency profiles as data grows.

| Approach | Queries | Total count | Deep pages | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Page<T>` + OFFSET | 2 (data + COUNT) | Yes | O(n) OFFSET scan | Small tables, 'Page 3 of 47' UI |
| `Slice<T>` + OFFSET | 1 | No | O(n) OFFSET scan | Medium tables, 'Load More' UI |
| `List<T>` + OFFSET | 1 | No | O(n) OFFSET scan | Scripts, admin tools |
| Keyset (cursor) | 1 | No | O(1) — index seek | Deep pagination, feeds, mobile APIs |

sections.title: Custom COUNT Queries and the OFFSET Performance Wall
sections.content:
**Optimizing the count separately:**

```java
@Query(value = "SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer WHERE o.status = :s",
       countQuery = "SELECT COUNT(o) FROM Order o WHERE o.status = :s")
Page<Order> findByStatusWithCustomer(@Param("s") OrderStatus status, Pageable p);
```

- **Default count** would include `JOIN FETCH customer` — wasted work; the count doesn't need it.
- **Explicit `countQuery`** removes the join — often **50-90% faster**.

**Why OFFSET fails at scale:**
- **`OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20`** forces the database to **scan and discard 10,000 rows** before returning your 20.
- At page 500, latency hits seconds.
- The database can't 'skip to row 10000' without reading the rows.

**Why keyset wins:**
- **`WHERE id > :lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`** uses an **index seek** — reads exactly 20 rows.
- **Constant time** regardless of page depth.
- Required for Twitter-style feeds, infinite scroll, mobile APIs.

**Caveat:**
- Keyset requires a **deterministic sort with a unique tiebreaker** (usually `id`).
- `ORDER BY createdAt` alone fails when two rows share a timestamp — cursor comparison is ambiguous.
- Always include `id` (or another unique column) as the **final sort key**.

sections.title: Keyset Pagination — Production Implementation
The Pagination Traps
sections.content:
**When pagination is fine:**
- Small tables (< 10K rows) — every strategy works; pick the simplest.
- 'Load More' UI — `Slice<T>` is ideal; no COUNT cost.
- Sort by `id` only — keyset is trivial.

**When pagination breaks:** - **JOIN FETCH + Pageable** — triggers `HHH90003004`; Hibernate loads every matching row, deduplicates, paginates in memory.
- Replace with `@EntityGraph` + `Pageable`.
- **Unstable sort orders** — `ORDER BY createdAt DESC` with ties produces duplicate rows across pages.
- Always add a unique tiebreaker.
- **Custom `@Query` without `countQuery`** — the auto-generated count is wrong for GROUP BY, HAVING, DISTINCT, UNION.
- **`Page<T>` on huge tables** — COUNT(*) on a 100M-row table can take seconds; switch to `Slice<T>` or keyset.

**Watch for:**
- **`PageRequest.of(0, Integer.MAX_VALUE)`** — anti-pattern; use `Stream<T>` with `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` for exports.
- **Mobile clients with retries** — keyset is robust to missed pages; OFFSET can skip or duplicate rows when data shifts.
- **Admin 'jump to page 500'** — OFFSET is painful; prefer date-range or keyset back-pagination.
- **Sort customization** — every sort field must be in the keyset cursor; user-customizable sort is harder with keyset.

**Production checklist:**
- `Page<T>` only when UI displays total count.
- `countQuery` explicit for every non-trivial `@Query` with `Page<T>`.
- Sort always has a unique tiebreaker.
- `@EntityGraph` instead of JOIN FETCH for paginated collections.
- Keyset for deep/infinite lists and feeds.
- `Stream<T>` + `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` for exports.

sections.title: Choosing a Strategy by Data Size, UI, and Sort
sections.content:
**By table size:**
- < 10K rows — any strategy; `Page<T>` + OFFSET is simplest.
- 10K – 1M rows — watch COUNT latency; prefer `Slice<T>` unless total is mandatory.
- 1M+ rows — OFFSET is O(n); **keyset is the only viable choice** for deep pagination.

**By UI pattern:**
- 'Page 3 of 47' bar — `Page<T>`; accept COUNT cost.
- 'Load More' / infinite scroll — `Slice<T>` or keyset.
- Export / batch — `Stream<T>` with `@Transactional(readOnly=true)` and JDBC fetch-size; constant memory.

**By sort:**
- Sort by `id` — keyset is trivial.
- Sort by `createdAt` — keyset needs `(createdAt, id)` compound cursor.
- User-customizable sort — keyset cursor grows; OFFSET can be acceptable on smaller tables.
- Multi-field sort — keyset works but cursor lexicographic comparison is complex.

**By user behavior:**
- Users browse first 5-10 pages — OFFSET is fine even at scale.
- Users jump to page 500 — keyset or 'jump to date' UX.
- Mobile clients with intermittent network — keyset; cursor encodes exact position.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Page<T>`** runs a COUNT; **`Slice<T>`** does not — choose by whether the UI needs the total.
- **`PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("createdAt").descending())`** — zero-indexed page number, combined with sort.
- **JOIN FETCH + Pageable** triggers `HHH90003004` — Hibernate paginates in memory; use `@EntityGraph` instead.
- **`Slice.hasNext()`** is computed by fetching `pageSize+1` rows.
- **Keyset pagination** is not built into Spring Data — implement with `@Query` and a compound `(createdAt, id)` cursor for constant-time deep pages.
- **`countQuery="..."`** lets you optimize the count separately when joins are unnecessary for counting.
- **`PageRequest.of(0, Integer.MAX_VALUE)`** is an anti-pattern — use `Stream<T>` with read-only transactions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Data's `Pageable` handles page number, size, and sort. The `Page` vs `Slice` choice has a real performance impact on large tables.

**`Page<T>` vs `Slice<T>`:**
- `Page<T>` — two queries: data with LIMIT/OFFSET and `SELECT COUNT(*)` for total
- `Slice<T>` — one query for `pageSize+1` rows; `hasNext()` is true if the extra row exists
- On a 10M-row table the COUNT alone can take seconds — pick `Slice<T>` unless total is required

**Creating Pageable:**
- `PageRequest.of(0, 20)` — zero-indexed
- `PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("createdAt").descending())` — with sort
- Spring MVC: `@PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "createdAt", direction = DESC) Pageable pageable` resolves from query params

**The JOIN FETCH + Pageable trap:**
- Fetching a `@OneToMany` with JOIN FETCH and Pageable triggers `HHH90003004`
- Hibernate loads all matching rows in memory and applies pagination in Java — latent OOM
- Use `@EntityGraph` instead — pagination applied in SQL, associations fetched via IN-clause batching

**Keyset pagination for scale:**
- OFFSET 10000 forces a scan of 10000 rows — O(n)
- `WHERE (createdAt, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId) ORDER BY createdAt DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20` is O(1)
- Required for feeds, infinite scroll, and any mobile API serving deep pagination
